item.title: What's the Meat of the Matter?
item.description:
🏛️ Independent Policy & Society • The India Forum

Author: Sayan Deori, Tanya Chaudhary, Shobhit Mahajan, Rahul Goel, Sudha Narayanan, Shree Saha, Aditi Gautam, Thomas Reardon, S. Gunasekaran, Seema Mundoli, Somdatta Karak, Salik Ahmad

Food is extremely political in India, embroiled in the larger politics of religion and caste. Over the last decade, these controversies have been further heightened. Basic nutritional food like eggs for children in schools has been scrapped in several states. Eating one’s favourite mutton curry during Hindu festivals may not be possible as the state shuts down meat shops during that period. Public spaces are segregated based on diet preferences, like when a mess in IIT Bombay introduced 'pure veg’ dining table. Vigilante mobs have raided kitchens and fridges on suspicion of beef consumption, and state diplomatic banquets have turned into ‘pure vegetarian’ galas. These are not isolated incidents, but connected events engineered and enabled by the current majoritarian Hindutva regime.

Karpagam highlights the caste angle of vegetarian food in India, and how the vegetarian imposition is carried out in India by the state...

The Meat of the Matter: How the Politics of Food Shapes Our Health by Sylvia Karpagam sits at the intersection of nutrition science and the politics of meat and animal source foods that is being played out in contemporary India. She enters the debate on the political and nutritional economy of food and the politics of idolising normative diets. Karpagam is a medical doctor and has faced online trolling for her views on food and nutrition, something she mentions in the book as well—these include casteist slurs like ‘rice bag convert’. Her book picks up questions related to food politics in contemporary India, and elaborates on them through a synthesis of evidence and data from published studies related to nutrition and public health.

The narrative thread of the book is the fictitious story of Princess Amudam of Arogya Nadu, a prosperous kingdom high on the Human Development Index, journeying to Starva Pradesh, a kingdom performing poorly on every variable of human development and public health. Along the princess’s passage between the kingdoms, Karapagam weaves in her account of contemporary Indian malnutrition and food issues. This story is threaded into all the chapters. The book can be broadly categorised into three categories for the readers: human nutrition, the burden of malnutrition, and the vegetarian and meat discourse that shapes policies.

The first three chapters provide a clinical register of human nutrition from the role of various macro- and micro-nutrients like proteins, fats, minerals and vitamins. They are textbook styled, outlining the scientific understanding of nutrients, their sources, and their bodily benefits, through fact-boxes of facts and blobs of information in sections like “Did You Know?” and “Debunking Myths on the Plate”. The end of each chapter has bulleted “Key Takeaways”. While it felt slightly stretchy at parts, the synthesis of nutritional science over many decades builds a coherent narrative on nutrition.

From nutrition science, Karpagam moves onto malnutrition, drawing on population level data and studies across time periods and regions. She illustrates the high burden of undernutrition in India and its indicators like stunting, wasting, and underweight, through the National Family Health Surveys (NFHS) and the Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS 2019). She also discusses the high prevalence of nutritional anaemia, mostly caused due to iron deficiency, to which women of reproductive age groups are the most vulnerable. Through these chapters, Karpagam also busts fads popular on social media, including 'Soya is Super Food', and  'Millets are Magical', through a careful explanation of nutrition bioavailability—how much of the theoretical nutrition of the food item the body can actually absorb—and dietary guidelines.

The third engagement of the book is with the politics of food and its manifestation in everyday life. Karpagam highlights the caste angle of vegetarian food in India, and how the vegetarian imposition is carried out in India by the state through ideological interference in public nutritional programmes. She highlights how concerns over ‘purity’ have caused eggs to be removed from midday meals in schools in several states.

In particular, she critiques the Akshya Patra Foundation (APF), whose collaboration with state governments in supplying school lunches promotes ‘sattvic food’. She mentions that “the foundation has a religious prerogative of advocating a de facto vegeterian diet, strictly avoiding meat, fish and eggs, and considers onions and garlic in food as lower modes of nature which inhibits spiritual advancement”. Not only this, but she also flags the APF’s financial opacity and its strong caste linkages and state patronages that it receives. These kinds of organisations are complicit in advancing and making a Hindutva state.

Karpagam challenges the narrative of the vegetarian discourse of nutrition by juxtaposing it with majoritarianism.

Karpagam also sheds light on the EAT-Lancet 2019 report and the “sustainable diet for planetary health” agenda that was being circulated and also platformed and promoted by India's food safety regulator. She touches upon the big food corporate nexus in nutrition policies. The EAT Lancet report 2019 propagated a global narrative to shift from a meat-based diet to a plant-based diet, and particularly idolised India as an ideal vegetarian society. She criticises the report's prescriptions: a clamp down on animal source foods, equating them as being as unhealthy as sugar, a hint at moving towards a plant based diet, and looking for “alternative proteins”. She mentions big corporations are privy to this and have appropriated the term “plant based”. Through reports like these, they manufacture new knowledge and consensus in creating systems that brings them more profits under the garb of science.

The Meat of the Matter provides a scientific understanding of major food and public health nutrition related controversies in India. Karpagam challenges the narrative of the vegetarian discourse of nutrition by juxtaposing it with majoritarianism. While she does not mention her methodology, or how she has collected her data, or selected her themes, this book can be read as a synthesis of the several structural harms that have been triggered by food and food cultures. I felt a deeper reading of the history of caste and violence in food politics and a critical perspective on policies that have led to our current nutritional systems could have been included. For instance, why do certain nutrients and foods become ‘heroes’ in certain decades or junctures. These include the rise of protein in the 1950s to the 70s, the micronutrients turn in the 90s, and later the emergence of ‘smarter foods’ like bio-fortification and fortification by nutrients. These events have shaped nutrition policies globally.

Although she mentions and acknowledges situated traditional knowledge of community in nourishment practices, we do not find in Karpagam's narrative a reference to the debates over how a biomedical approach to malnutrition can be a problematic hegemony, especially for countries in the Global South, where land dispossession, colonisation, caste location and socio economic factors shape nutrition. Yet, the accessible language used to present the science makes The Meat of the Matter an important book for people to understand food and nutrition politics in India.

Sayan Deori is a PhD scholar at Tezpur University, Assam. 

Independent Source: The India Forum

item.title: Govt cuts wheat allocation in weekly auction even as millers ready to pay over ₹31/Kg
item.description:
🇮🇳 Indian Economy • The Hindu BusinessLine

The government has reduced the overall wheat allocation for sales in weekly auction, to be held on October 28, by 5,000 tonnes to 1.01 lakh tonnes (lt) compared to the previous tender even as processors and millers have scrambled to buy the grain at over ₹3,100/quintal in many States when the all India average wholesale price now stands at ₹2,910/quintal.

Millers have suggested to the government that it should progressively increase the quantity in the weekly auction since open market availability is stressed and millers are now dependent on Food Corporation of India (FCI) for supplies, according to industry sources.

“It seems there is not as much wheat in the market as was earlier thought and hence, the millers wanted to buy as much as they could from the government auction,” Dharmendra Jain, President of Roller Flour Millers’ Federation of India told businessline. He also said that the Federation has suggested to the government that it should increase the quantity in the weekly auctions.

In the bids floated by State offices of FCI in Assam, Odisha, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Bihar and Kerala, the allocation for the latest round is about 11,900 tonnes lower than the auction held on October 21. While there may be justification for reduction of quota for Odisha to 3,500 tonnes as millers could buy only 3,050 tonnes out of 6,000 tonnes quantity offered in last round, the same does not hold true for many of the other States.

Maximum offtake

Millers in States such as Assam, Karnataka and Telanga are wondering why the government cut their allocation despite maximum offtake, another source noted. For instance, out of 8,000 tonnes wheat offered in Assam in the last round, millers were successful to buy 7,940 tonnes. Similarly, in Telangana, 3,460 tonnes were bought out of 3,500 and in Karnataka 5,430 tonnes out of 6,000 tonnes in last round. This time, the government has allocated a much lower 5,000 tonnes for Assam, 1,000 tonnes for Telangana and 5,000 tonnes for Karnataka.

On the other hand, there is a total increase of 6,450 tonnes in Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Himachal Pradesh, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab from the quantity allocated on October 16.

Punjab has got maximum allocation of 25,000 tonnes against 23,000 tonnes in last round as there were 204 successful processors/millers who offered to buy wheat between ₹3,065/quintal and ₹2,861/quintal. As much as 8,970 tonnes of wheat were sold at ₹3,000/quintal or higher rates to 72 buyers in the State.

“The offered quantity in a single depot should be decided based on the concentration of mills in the surrounding areas rather than putting a maximum cap of 500 tonne per week. For instance, Ludhiana has 18 mills having 20 per cent share in Punjab’s total flour milling capacity and it still gets same allocation as compared to other depots where there is lower demand,” said Naresh Ghai, President of Roller Flour Mills Association of Punjab.

Besides restructuring the maximum cap, the weekly allocation for Punjab should be hiked to 40,000 tonnes, Ghai said adding there is zero arrival of wheat in Punjab’s mandis. He also does not foresee easing of wheat prices.

The FCI had 479.92 lt wheat stock as on September 1, which is the highest on the date in last five years. The stock was 517.87 lt on September 1, 2021. The government had procured 357.57 lt of wheat in 2026-27 season against 299.75 lt in the previous marketing season (RMS 2025-26). India’s wheat production in 2025-26 crop year rose to record 120.66 million tonnes (mt) from 117.95 mt in the previous year.

Published on October 25, 2026

Source: The Hindu BusinessLine

item.title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
item.description:
🌍 Major Global Event • The Guardian Economics

VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.

The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.

Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.

Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.

It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.

Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.

The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.

Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.

However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

item.title: Nvidia open-sources Flora to make robot video labeling 125x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra
item.description:
🤖 AI & Tech • The Decoder
Plus AI research
Copy the url to clipboard Share this article Go to comment section
Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper
Oct 25, 2026
Nvidia

Labeling one hour of robot video for 72 cents instead of $88 is what Nvidia promises with Flora, its open data engine. But the comparison with GPT-6 Astra isn't quite as lopsided as the price tag suggests.

Large AI models for robots learn from videos that need text annotations, and according to Nvidia's GEAR research lab, this requires three types of labels. First, descriptions of what action happens when in the video, used to select training data. Second, ratings of how well a robot progresses step by step, so it can learn through trial and error. And third, judgments on whether a task was completed successfully, used to monitor robots during deployment. Most existing tools only provide one of these types. Large language models like GPT-6 Astra can generate several, but they're too expensive for the massive volumes of video involved.

According to the paper, Flora covers all three. Nvidia says the system is already running during training of its GR00T models, annotating up to 200,000 hours of video per day across 512 GB300 GPUs. The models are available on Hugging Face.

Flora consists of three fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models. A 9B model splits videos into action segments, and a 27B model describes them while factoring in what happened before and after each action. A second 27B model called Flora-Rewarder takes on three roles depending on the prompt. It rates an episode's success on a scale of 1 to 5, classifies each half-second step as normal, suboptimal, or failure, and assigns scores based on self-defined rubrics.

Up to 125x cheaper by Nvidia's own estimates

In a test with 50 videos, Flora scored slightly better than GPT-6 Astra according to Nvidia, even though OpenAI's model was allowed to use its full reasoning capacity. Labeling one hour of video runs about 72 cents with Flora by Nvidia's estimate, compared to roughly $88.50 with GPT-6 Astra. Claude Opus 5 scored much worse in the same test and still cost about $42 per hour.

The Flora cost figures are projections, though, not production measurements. Nvidia calculated them based on an assumed rental price of $10 per GPU per hour.

Flora finds actions better, but Astra often describes them more precisely

On the public WGO-Bench, Flora is best at detecting action boundaries but trails Astra in overall score and falls behind Gemini 3.8 Flash in pure description accuracy. According to the researchers, the gains come mainly from temporal localization.

On Nvidia's own DenseCaptionBench, Flora leads across all metrics for human recordings, but for robot videos the model comes in second behind Astra. There's a methodological catch the researchers acknowledge, too. GPT-6 Astra evaluates the descriptions while also being one of the models under test.

Almost no other model catches mid-episode errors

On RoboRewardBench, Flora's error rate is 27.8 percent lower than Astra's. The paper attributes the gap to partially completed tasks. When a robot only tips a bottle over instead of knocking it off the table, Flora assigns 3 out of 5 points to match the human reference, while Astra gives just one.

Flora-Rewarder catches 53.3 percent of failed steps within an episode, while no competitor gets above 11.7 percent and Astra doesn't catch a single one. The tradeoff is that Flora falsely flags about 11 percent of normal steps as errors. Astra still leads on rubric-based scoring and trajectory ranking.

In a video with many short hand movements, Flora identifies 34 of 37 individual actions, while Astra catches only four. On the flip side, Flora sometimes splits longer actions into too many small steps and occasionally gets descriptions wrong. In one video, a robot hand wipes a plate with a cloth, but Flora describes it as folding a napkin.

Nvidia positions Flora as an open alternative to commercial services like Scale AI's Physical AI Data Engine. Researchers can use it to scale their own robotics datasets and test approaches like transferring human demonstrations to robots. Nvidia is investing billions in open AI models to keep developers in its hardware ecosystem and drive demand for its chips, and Flora serves that same goal.

The company has also been working for some time to offset the shortage of robotics training data through simulation and automated data processing. At GTC earlier this year, Nvidia showed a data pipeline that automatically prepares, multiplies, and scores training material. Flora adds detailed labels and reward signals from video to that pipeline.

All of this feeds into Nvidia's strategy of covering the entire robotics value chain, from hardware and training data to simulation and the AI models themselves. Google's recently announced Gemini 4 Argon targets a similar part of the robotics training process, also identifying work steps in training videos and flagging failed actions.
